sweep_summary: Ket (kett1243) is in the catalog as kind=lexical, deciding source Georg 2007:58-60 (held PDF). The sweep's two title hits are both first-hand, on-topic, and unread: Vajda 2000 'Ket Prosodic Phonology' (Lincom, 22 pp.) has no open copy anywhere reached (no HathiTrust item, Google Books no preview, Georg's 2002 Language book notice paywalled at DOI 10.1353/lan.2002.0156, Vajda's WWU site gone and Wayback offline), and Werner 1996 'Vergleichende Akzentologie der Jenissej-Sprachen' (Harrassowitz, viii+168 pp.) is HathiTrust search-only (mdp.39015041372171) and Harvard offsite print. Second-hand evidence from held sources fixes what they contain: Georg 2007 cites Vajda 2000:2 (monosyllabic tone diagrams) and :20 (phonological-word boundaries) and, at p.60 fn.70, says 'Much of the following [the polysyllabic accent account] is based on' Werner 1996's experimental data (diagrams from Werner 1996:58, :60; exceptions at :66ff.); Nefedov 2015 cites Vajda 2000:4-8 and Werner 1996:66ff. Both items therefore get priority high, Werner 1996 first, as the empirical base of the catalog's deciding statement. Re-reading Georg 2007 p.58/p.60 confirms the catalog coding (two contours on the first two syllables of the phonological word, fifth/initial as default, sixth/second-syllable lexically and morphologically restricted); nothing read contradicts it. Crossref, Glottolog, Open Library, archive.org search and the HathiTrust catalog API were used instead.

new_statements.quote: p.60: 'The prosodic behaviour of tri-, quadrisyllabic and longer morpheme chains is more complicated and has not been subject to intense scrutiny[70]. Only few fairly recurrent patterns can be mentioned here, possibly only tendencies. The default rule is that the first two syllables of the phonological word receive one of the two disyllabic contours described above, leaving any syllable further to the right as a toneless appendix; most common is the fifth contour' — fn.70: 'However, Werner 1996 must be mentioned, where a great number of empirical data has been assembled. Much of the following is based on this source and its examples'.

new_statements.locator: p.58 (disyllabic contours, minimal pairs) and p.60 with fn.70, sec. 3.1.3 'Tone/accent in polysyllabic words'
new_statements.reading: This is the catalog's existing deciding source, re-read at page level in this sweep (no first-hand text of either sweep item was obtainable). It states that a Ket phonological word of two or more syllables carries one of two pitch contours on its first two syllables: the 'fifth' contour (rise on syllable 1, fall on syllable 2; 'acoustic impression... of a dynamic accent on the first syllable', p.57), which is the default and most common, versus the rarer 'sixth' contour (peak on syllable 2), whose choice is 'largely unpredictable' and lexically/morphologically tied (compounds, some plurals; minimal pairs ásel 'snowshoe' : àsel 'ilimka-boat', qóqbun 'cuckoo' : qòqbun 'cuckoos', p.58). That confirms the catalog's kind=lexical with the {10…0, 010…0} rule set and an initial dominant pattern. The new information from this sweep is provenance: Georg explicitly bases his polysyllabic account on Werner 1996's instrumental data (fn.70; diagrams from Werner 1996:58 and :60), so Werner 1996 — a sweep item — is the primary empirical source behind the deciding source and is the top acquisition target, ahead of Vajda 2000.

The "sixth" contour is considerably rarer'; :60 'The default rule is that the first two syllables of the phonological word receive one of the two disyllabic contours... most common is the fifth contour'; Nefedov 2015:15 (after Vajda 2004:13) 'rising/falling pitch resembling word-initial stress' as the general case with second-syllable peak only in 'a few disyllabic words'; Vajda 2009 (WOLD) 'characteristically have a rising falling tone on the first two moras'. This also explains (without endorsing) StressTyp2's 'initial' code. Also fill the empty quote/cite/loc/grade fields from dq/dloc (Georg 2007:58-60).

sources.quote: Werner 1997:179: "Stress in words is free: sabot 'belongings', assano '...', usdlgat '(little) birches'. In the stressed syllable dynamic characteristics prevail, except in the realization of two special disyllabic accentual types: in one of them a rise of the fundamental pitch of the voice is observed on the first (stressed) syllable, in the other on the last (stressed) syllable, with equal intensity on both syllables: qorqun 'cuckoo', plural qorqun."
